summary.text: After division by \((n-1)!\), fixed-\(k\) binomial asymptotics show that only the \(j=0\) part of the inner inclusion–exclusion sum survives, giving \((-2)^k/k!\); a summable exponential-series bound permits termwise passage to the limit, so the normalized count tends to \(\sum_{k\ge0}(-2)^k/k!=e^{-2}\) (and taking the absolute value does not change this positive limit). The proposed expression has the same normalized limit because its correction series tends to zero by dominated convergence and \(n/(n-2)\to1\), so the ratio of the two expressions tends to one.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 (x)_r=x(x-1)\cdots(x-r+1)
\]
denote the falling factorial, with \((x)_0=1\). For nonnegative integers \(N,r\), we also use
\[
 (N)_r=r!\binom Nr.
\]
As usual, \(\binom Nr=0\) when \(r>N\).

We begin with the exact inclusion–exclusion formula for the sequence. For \(n\leq 5\), put \(a(n)=0\). For \(n>5\), define
\[
 I(n,k)=
 \sum_{j=\max(0,k+5-n)}^{\min(k,4)}
 \binom{8-j}{j}\binom{2n-k+j-10}{k-j}
\]
and
\[
 S(n)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(-1)^k(n-1-k)!\,I(n,k).
\]
The exact formula for A258667 is
\[
 a(n)=|S(n)|.
\]
This is the inclusion–exclusion count for the stated ménage seating problem after the mathematician has chosen the chair nine seats clockwise from his wife. Thus it remains to determine the asymptotic behavior of this exact finite sum.

Define, for all \(n,k\geq 0\),
\[
 u_{n,k}=
 \begin{cases}
 (-1)^k\dfrac{(n-1-k)!}{(n-1)!}I(n,k),&n>5\text{ and }k<n,\\[6pt]
 0,&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}
\]
For \(n\geq6\), only \(0\leq k<n\) contribute, and therefore
\[
 \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}u_{n,k}=\frac{S(n)}{(n-1)!}.
\tag{1}
\]
We will evaluate the limit of the series on the left by dominated convergence.

First fix \(k\). If \(n\geq k+5\), the lower endpoint \(\max(0,k+5-n)\) in the definition of \(I(n,k)\) is zero. Also,
\[
 \frac{(n-1-k)!}{(n-1)!}=\frac1{(n-1)_k}.
\tag{2}
\]
Consequently, for all sufficiently large \(n\),
\[
 u_{n,k}=(-1)^k
 \sum_{j=0}^{\min(k,4)}
 \binom{8-j}{j}
 \frac{\binom{2n-k+j-10}{k-j}}{(n-1)_k}.
\tag{3}
\]
We now find the limit of each term in this finite sum.

For fixed integers \(k,j\) with \(0\leq j\leq k\), set \(r=k-j\). As \(n\to\infty\),
\[
 2n-k+j-10\sim 2n,
\]
so the standard fixed-order binomial asymptotic gives
\[
 \binom{2n-k+j-10}{r}
 \sim \frac{(2n)^r}{r!}.
\tag{4}
\]
Likewise, for fixed \(k\),
\[
 (n-1)_k\sim n^k.
\tag{5}
\]
It follows from (4) and (5) that
\[
 \frac{\binom{2n-k+j-10}{k-j}}{(n-1)_k}
 \sim \frac{2^{k-j}}{(k-j)!}n^{-j}.
\]
Thus the actual limit is
\[
 \lim_{n\to\infty}
 \frac{\binom{2n-k+j-10}{k-j}}{(n-1)_k}
 =
 \begin{cases}
 \dfrac{2^k}{k!},&j=0,\\[6pt]
 0,&j>0.
 \end{cases}
\tag{6}
\]
In (3), therefore, every term with \(j>0\) disappears in the limit. The coefficient of the \(j=0\) term is \(\binom80=1\). Hence
\[
 \lim_{n\to\infty}u_{n,k}
 =(-1)^k\frac{2^k}{k!}
 =\frac{(-2)^k}{k!}.
\tag{7}
\]

To pass the limit through the infinite sum over \(k\), we need a bound independent of \(n\). We establish the required estimate explicitly. Let \(0\leq j\leq k<n\), and again put \(r=k-j\). The falling factorial in the numerator satisfies
\[
 (2n+j-k-10)_r\leq 2^r(n-1)_r.
\tag{8}
\]
Indeed, writing each falling factorial as a product indexed by \(0\leq i<r\), the corresponding factors satisfy
\[
 2n+j-k-10-i\leq 2(n-1-i).
\]
If subtraction causes a left-hand factor to be zero, the inequality is automatic; otherwise it is the displayed elementary linear inequality, using \(j\leq k\). Multiplication of these nonnegative factorwise inequalities proves (8).

Furthermore, because \(r\leq k\leq n-1\),
\[
 (n-1)_r\leq(n-1)_k.
\tag{9}
\]
To see this, write
\[
 (n-1)_k=(n-1)_r\,(n-1-r)_{k-r}.
\]
Every factor in the second falling factorial is a positive integer, so that factor is at least one.

Using \((N)_r=r!\binom Nr\), inequalities (8) and (9) give
\[
 \binom{2n+j-k-10}{r}\,r!
 =(2n+j-k-10)_r
 \leq 2^r(n-1)_r
 \leq 2^r(n-1)_k.
\]
After division by the positive quantity \(r!(n-1)_k\), we obtain
\[
 0\leq
 \frac{\binom{2n+j-k-10}{k-j}}{(n-1)_k}
 \leq \frac{2^{k-j}}{(k-j)!}.
\tag{10}
\]

Define
\[
 B_k=\sum_{j=0}^{4}
 \binom{8-j}{j}\,
 \mathbf 1_{\{j\leq k\}}
 \frac{2^{k-j}}{(k-j)!},
\tag{11}
\]
where the indicator makes a term zero when \(j>k\). The summands in the inner sum defining \(I(n,k)\) are nonnegative. Therefore (10), the triangle inequality, and enlargement of the actual range of \(j\) to \(0\leq j\leq4\) show that, for every \(n\geq6\) and every \(k\),
\[
 |u_{n,k}|\leq B_k.
\tag{12}
\]
For \(k\geq n\), the left side is zero, so this includes that case as well.

The sequence \((B_k)\) is summable. Indeed, for each fixed \(j\in\{0,1,2,3,4\}\), shifting the index \(m=k-j\) gives
\[
 \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}
 \mathbf 1_{\{j\leq k\}}
 \frac{2^{k-j}}{(k-j)!}
 =\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\frac{2^m}{m!}=e^2.
\]
Since (11) is a sum of only five constant multiples of these shifted exponential series,
\[
 \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}B_k<\infty.
\tag{13}
\]

Equations (7), (12), and (13) allow the dominated-convergence theorem for series to be applied. We conclude that
\[
 \lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}u_{n,k}
 =\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-2)^k}{k!}
 =e^{-2}.
\tag{14}
\]
By (1), this says
\[
 \frac{S(n)}{(n-1)!}\longrightarrow e^{-2}.
\tag{15}
\]
The sequence itself is \(a(n)=|S(n)|\). Since \((n-1)!>0\),
\[
 \frac{a(n)}{(n-1)!}
 =\left|\frac{S(n)}{(n-1)!}\right|.
\]
Taking limits in (15), and using \(e^{-2}>0\), yields
\[
 \boxed{\displaystyle
 \frac{a(n)}{(n-1)!}\longrightarrow e^{-2}.}
\tag{16}
\]
Notice that this argument does not require a separate proof that the signed inclusion–exclusion expression is eventually positive: taking absolute values is continuous, and its limiting value is already positive.

We next analyze the more precise expression appearing on the right-hand side of the conjecture. For each \(n\), interpret its series correction as the finite sum
\[
 q_n=\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\frac{(-1)^k}{k!(n-1)_k}.
\tag{17}
\]
This is the relevant meaning of the displayed \(\sum_{k\geq1}\) for integer \(n\): once \(k\geq n\), the falling factorial \((n-1)_k\) vanishes, so only the naturally defined terms with \(k<n\) are retained. We claim that
\[
 q_n\longrightarrow0.
\tag{18}
\]

For completeness, this is another direct dominated-convergence argument. Extend the summand by zero and define
\[
 v_{n,k}=
 \begin{cases}
 \dfrac{(-1)^k}{k!(n-1)_k},&1\leq k<n,\\[6pt]
 0,&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}
\]
Then \(q_n=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}v_{n,k}\). For each fixed \(k\geq1\), the denominator \((n-1)_k\sim n^k\) tends to infinity, so
\[
 v_{n,k}\longrightarrow0.
\]
For \(k=0\), the term is identically zero. Also, whenever \(1\leq k<n\), the positive integer \((n-1)_k\) is at least one, and hence
\[
 |v_{n,k}|=\frac1{k!(n-1)_k}\leq\frac1{k!}.
\tag{19}
\]
The same inequality is trivial when \(v_{n,k}=0\). Since
\[
 \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac1{k!}=e<\infty,
\]
dominated convergence gives
\[
 \lim_{n\to\infty}q_n
 =\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}0=0,
\]
which proves (18). In particular,
\[
 1+q_n\longrightarrow1.
\tag{20}
\]

Now let
\[
 T_n=e^{-2}\frac{n!}{n-2}(1+q_n)
\tag{21}
\]
for \(n>2\); its value at the finitely many smaller integers is irrelevant to asymptotics. Normalize this expression by the same factor \((n-1)!\) used above. Since \(n!=n(n-1)!\),
\[
 \frac{T_n}{(n-1)!}
 =e^{-2}\frac{n}{n-2}(1+q_n).
\tag{22}
\]
As \(n\to\infty\),
\[
 \frac{n}{n-2}\longrightarrow1,
\]
and (20) gives \(1+q_n\to1\). Thus (22) implies
\[
 \boxed{\displaystyle
 \frac{T_n}{(n-1)!}\longrightarrow e^{-2}.}
\tag{23}
\]

Finally, divide (16) by (23). The limiting denominator is the nonzero number \(e^{-2}\), so \(T_n/(n-1)!\) is nonzero for all sufficiently large \(n\), and
\[
 \frac{a(n)}{T_n}
 =
 \frac{a(n)/(n-1)!}{T_n/(n-1)!}
 \longrightarrow\frac{e^{-2}}{e^{-2}}=1.
\]
Therefore
\[
 a(n)\sim e^{-2}\frac{n!}{n-2}
 \left(1+\sum_{k\geq1}\frac{(-1)^k}{k!(n-1)_k}\right),
\]
where, for each integer \(n\), the correction sum is understood as the finite sum over \(1\leq k<n\). This is the asserted asymptotic equivalence.
